Scott County sits in Central Kentucky with Georgetown as its county seat. It is one of the faster growing counties in the state, which makes it a county many investors watch. In Kentucky, Scott County sells delinquent real property taxes as tax lien certificates, called certificates of delinquency, not tax deeds. This guide explains when Scott County tax sales are usually held, how registration works, where the sale happens, what returns investors can expect, and what due diligence steps matter most before you buy.

What is Scott County’s tax lien investing system?

Scott County follows Kentucky’s certificate of delinquency system. That means investors buy the unpaid tax lien, not the property itself. The county clerk handles the sale after delinquent bills move over from the sheriff. Kentucky says most county clerk tax sales happen from mid July through the end of August, and Scott County’s own timeline shows its sale has been held in late August at 8:30 a.m. Recent county sale notices also show a late August sale date, which fits the state schedule.

Important Details

Key Takeaways

  • Scott County in Kentucky sells tax lien certificates called certificates of delinquency, not tax deeds.
  • The typical tax sale occurs in late August at 8:30 a.m. in Georgetown, with a fixed interest rate of 12%.
  • Investors must register in advance and conduct due diligence on properties and owners before purchasing liens.
  • The county benefits from economic growth, major employers like Toyota, and strong transportation access through I-75 and I-64.
  • Scott County is appealing for tax lien investors due to its structured system, clear rules, and potential for significant returns.

Fun Facts About the County

  • Scott County’s population is over 60,000 based on recent Census estimates.
  • Georgetown is the county seat and is tied closely to horse culture and auto manufacturing.
  • The county sits along I 75 and I 64, which helps access and growth.
  • Toyota has a major manufacturing presence tied to the local economy.

Attractions & Economic Highlights

  • Kentucky Horse Park is nearby and helps drive visitor traffic.
  • Toyota plant tours and horse related tourism give the county broad appeal.
  • I 75 and I 64 cross near Georgetown, which supports transport and business access.
  • Manufacturing, tourism, horse activity, and local retail all support the area.

Why This County is Ideal for Tax Lien Investors

  • Scott County sits in a growth area near Lexington with strong road access.
  • Kentucky tax lien certificates earn up to 12% simple interest, which is better than many low risk savings options.
  • Investors buy a lien, not the house, which can lower some purchase risk when compared with direct deed buying.
  • A county with active housing demand and strong employers can make tax lien research more useful because many parcels have real market use.

Auction Process for Tax Lien Sales

Scott County uses Kentucky’s certificate of delinquency sale process. This is not a bid down interest auction. The interest rate is set by law. The sale is about who gets to buy which liens, not who accepts a lower return. Kentucky rules require advance registration, lists of desired certificates, and deposits. Priority certificates are handled first. Then the rest are sold by random draw and lot selection.

How the Auction Works

Here is a simple look at how the tax lien auction works from registration through post-sale compliance

  1. Register before the deadline

    Third party buyers must register with the county clerk before the sale. State-level registration may also be needed if your purchase volume crosses the Kentucky thresholds.

  2. Submit your certificate lists

    Buyers can submit a list of priority certificates and a list of current year certificates they want to buy.

  3. Fund your deposit

    Kentucky rules allow the clerk to require deposits based on the certificates requested.

  4. Priority liens go first

    If a buyer already holds a prior year lien on the same parcel, that buyer can get priority rights to the new lien.

  5. Random draw sets order

    For the remaining liens, registered buyers draw numbers on sale day. Lowest number picks first.

  6. Buy in lots

    Kentucky rules use lot sizes based on how many certificates are in the sale. Smaller counties can sell in lots of up to five.

  7. Pay the balance

    After deposits are applied, the buyer must pay the rest by the clerk’s deadline.

Maximum Potential Returns and Expected Returns on Scott County Tax Lien Certificates

The headline return in Scott County is the same as the rest of Kentucky. A certificate of delinquency bears 12% simple interest per year, which is also described by the state as 1% per month. That is the legal rate, so investors do not bid the rate down at the sale. Expected returns depend on when the owner redeems, how clean the file is, and whether extra collection costs apply later under Kentucky law. The cleanest outcome is a prompt redemption with minimal delay. The best long run cases are liens attached to usable property with a strong owner incentive to pay.

Open to All Investors / Foreign Investor Participation

Kentucky allows third party purchasers to register and buy certificates of delinquency. State materials describe eligible purchasers broadly and require state registration only when purchase counts or dollar volume rise above the thresholds. The rules focus on registration, related party limits, deposits, and compliance. They do not limit participation to Scott County residents. That is why both local and out of state investors can take part if they meet the rules. For foreign investors, the practical issue is not location. It is paperwork, compliance, and the ability to manage notices, records, and later collection work.

Importance of Due Diligence in Scott County Tax Lien Investing

Due diligence matters because a Kentucky tax lien is a lien purchase, not a promise of easy profit. You still need to study the parcel, the owner, and the records.

What Due Diligence Entails

  • Check the Scott County PVA record for owner name and parcel details.
  • Review deed and lien records at the Scott County Clerk.
  • Study access, use, occupancy, and property condition from maps and site visits.
  • Compare the tax amount with local resale demand and real value trends.
  • Know your post-sale notice and collection duties under Kentucky law.

Risks of Skipping Due Diligence

  • You may buy a lien on land with poor access or weak resale value.
  • You may miss title issues or other recorded problems.
  • You may overestimate how fast the owner will redeem.
  • You may underestimate the time needed before stronger collection action can start.

Buying Over-the-Counter liens in Scott County

How to Purchase OTC Liens

Kentucky allows an eligible third-party purchaser to buy prior-year certificates of delinquency outside the annual current-year sale. State guidance says once a purchaser is eligible, prior year certificates may be acquired at any time. In practice, ask the Scott County Clerk what prior year certificates are still held and what registration documents are required before purchase.

Benefits of OTC Purchases

OTC style prior year purchases can be easier because there is no sale day rush. You can focus on records, parcel quality, and file review before committing funds. The statutory interest framework still matters.

Why Scott County is a Top Choice for Tax Lien Investors

Economic and Tax Advantages

  • Strong road links through I 75 and I 64 support commerce.
  • Large employers like Toyota add economic stability.
  • Kentucky’s fixed 12% rate gives a clear return model.

Real Estate Market Overview

Scott County benefits from Lexington area growth, employer demand, and a mix of suburban and rural property. That gives investors more parcel types to study than in some very small rural counties. Still, not every lien is equal. Good returns usually come from good records and careful parcel screening, not from buying every certificate on the list.

Conclusion

Scott County, Kentucky is a solid county for tax lien investors who want a clear rules based system. The county sells certificates of delinquency, not deeds. Sales are usually held in late summer. The interest rate is fixed by law at 12% simple interest. The county clerk handles registration and sale logistics, while Kentucky law controls the broader process. For many investors, that means a clean path to high returns with a lower risk profile than direct deed speculation. Still, the smart play is always the same. Study the parcel. Review the records. Know the notice rules. And buy with a plan.

Pro Tips

  • Focus on parcels near growth corridors around Georgetown first. Transport access can matter later.
  • Pull both PVA data and clerk records before sale day. One source alone is not enough.
  • Do not treat all late August sales the same. Confirm Scott County’s exact posted deadline each year.
  • Build your bid list by property quality, not just tax amount due.
  • If you already hold an older Scott County lien, check for priority rights before the new sale.

FAQs for Scott County Tax Liens

Do I get the property right away?

No. You buy the tax lien certificate, not the deed.

Can I start foreclosure right after the sale?

No. Kentucky allows action after one year.

Do I need a quiet title action after buying the lien?

Not at lien stage. That issue comes later only if foreclosure leads to title transfer.

Can I finance improvements before I own the property?

No. You should not improve property you do not own.

Can other liens or issues still matter?

Yes. That is why record review and title research matter.
